rd-school-c10-english-a.fp-triumph-surge.title: A Triumph of Surgery — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-a.fp-triumph-surge.subtitle: A pampered Pekingese, a loving but foolish owner, and a vet whose 'surgery' needed no knife at all

sections.h: A hook: can love make someone ill?
sections.md:
A little dog lies on a silk cushion, so fat he can barely walk, eyes bloodshot, tongue lolling. He is surrounded by cream cakes, chocolates and malt. His owner, a wealthy widow, weeps that he must be dreadfully ill. The vet looks at the dog, then at the overflowing plates, and knows exactly what the disease is: **too much love**.

*A Triumph of Surgery* comes from the warm, funny memoirs of **James Herriot** — the pen name of **James Alfred Wight** (1916–1995), a Scottish-born vet who practised in the Yorkshire Dales in England. His books, beginning with *If Only They Could Talk* (1970) and collected in *All Creatures Great and Small*, made millions of readers fall in love with country animals and their owners.

The chapter is in the supplementary reader **Footprints without Feet**. It is told by Herriot himself in the first person.

**Key idea:** pampering is not the same as caring. Real love sometimes means saying 'no'.
keyTerms: veterinary surgeon (vet) — doctor for animals
pampered — given too much comfort and indulgence
memoir — true account of the writer's experiences

sections.md:
**Mrs Pumphrey** is a rich, kind-hearted lady who loves her Pekingese dog **Tricki** with all her heart. But her love is **foolish**. She treats Tricki like a spoilt child.

One day Herriot sees them walking in the street. He is **shocked**: Tricki is hugely fat, like a bloated sausage with a leg at each corner. His eyes are bloodshot and rheumy; his tongue lolls from his jaws. Mrs Pumphrey explains that Tricki is listless and has no energy — so she has been giving him **extra snacks** to build him up: **malt, cod-liver oil** and **Horlicks** at bedtime. She has also been giving him **cream cakes** and **chocolates** because he loves them so much.

Herriot advises her firmly: cut down on sweet things, give him plenty of **exercise** and a **strict diet**. Mrs Pumphrey promises; she seems to understand.

But she cannot resist Tricki's pleading eyes. She doesn't keep her word.

**Character note:** Mrs Pumphrey is not cruel — she is *over-indulgent*. Her love blinds her to what is good for the dog. Think of parents who give children unlimited junk food or screen time 'out of love'.

options: Because she thought he was weak and needed building up
Because the vet told her to

sections.md:
A few days later Herriot receives a **panic-stricken call** from Mrs Pumphrey. Tricki has stopped eating, refuses even his favourite dishes, and has bouts of **vomiting**. He spends all his time lying on a rug, panting. He doesn't want to go for walks or do anything.

Herriot drives to the house. Tricki is lying on his cushion, barely able to raise his head. Herriot decides on a plan and announces that Tricki must be **hospitalised** — taken to the surgery for **observation**, for about **two weeks**. Mrs Pumphrey is horrified: how will her darling survive without her? But she agrees.

As Tricki is carried to the car, a little procession follows: servants bring his **day bed, night bed, favourite cushions, toys and rubber rings, breakfast bowl, lunch bowl, supper bowl**, and his coats! Herriot, realising the car is filling up, drives off as quickly as he can before more is loaded. Mrs Pumphrey wails and waves her handkerchief as if her dog were going to war.

**The 'surgery' of the title** is an ironic word: in Britain, a doctor's or vet's clinic is called a *surgery*. Herriot will perform **no operation** at all.

check.q: Why did Herriot take Tricki to his surgery?
options: To keep him away from Mrs Pumphrey's over-feeding and observe him
check.why: Herriot knew the illness came from overfeeding, so separating Tricki from his indulgent owner was the real cure.

sections.h: The cure: no food, lots of play
sections.md:
At the surgery, Herriot lays Tricki on the floor and examines him. The dog is grossly overweight but has no real disease. Herriot's treatment is simple:

- **No food** for **two days** — only plenty of **water**.
- Then gradually, a sensible diet.
- **Exercise** — Tricki is put among the other dogs: a pack of big, healthy dogs who rush around the house and garden.

By the end of the second day Tricki begins to show **interest** in his surroundings. On the third day he starts whimpering at the sight of food. He joins the other dogs and they become friends. He begins to **romp** around the garden, getting knocked over by the big dogs and getting up to rejoin the fun. At mealtimes he fights for his share at the common bowl. Within days he is a happy, lively little dog, transformed. He is accepted as a member of the gang — 'an unlikely silky little object among the shaggy crew'.

**Science note:** obesity in dogs is a real veterinary problem. Excess fat strains the heart and joints, and too many treats cause digestive upsets. Vets recommend measured food, no chocolate (it is **toxic to dogs** because of theobromine), and daily exercise.

sections.h: The comedy of the eggs and wine
sections.md:
Meanwhile, Mrs Pumphrey is desperate with worry. She **telephones** several times a day for news. She also starts sending **food** to help Tricki recover: **fresh eggs** — two dozen at a time — to build up his strength. Soon she adds bottles of **wine** (she sends **port** — no, in the story it is **two bottles of** **sherry**? — the textbook says she sends **wine** and later **brandy**) to build up his blood.

Here is where Herriot's humour shines. He and his partners do not give the eggs and wine to Tricki — they **enjoy them themselves**! Herriot writes that the eggs became part of the household's breakfast, and the bottles of wine made the evenings cheerful. The days began to pass in a haze of good living for the vets. He confesses that he was tempted to keep Tricki longer than necessary because the treats were so welcome.

But he knows what is right. Tricki is fit, and it is time to return him.

**Note for exams:** NCERT asks whether Herriot was *unethical* in keeping the food. Most readers see it as harmless comedy: the food would have harmed Tricki, and Herriot gives an honest, self-mocking account. You can argue either way, giving reasons.

check.q: What did Herriot do with the eggs and wine Mrs Pumphrey sent for Tricki?
options: He and his partners enjoyed them
check.why: Knowing the rich food would harm Tricki, Herriot and his colleagues consumed the eggs and wine themselves, which he describes humorously.

sections.md:
Herriot telephones Mrs Pumphrey to collect Tricki. She arrives in her chauffeur-driven car within minutes. When Tricki sees her, he **leaps** from Herriot's arms into her lap, licking her face and barking happily, wagging his tail. He bounds around full of energy — a completely transformed dog.

Mrs Pumphrey is **overjoyed**. With tears in her eyes she cries that this is **a triumph of surgery!** She believes Herriot has performed some miraculous medical treatment.

The **irony** is delicious: there was **no surgery at all**, only a common-sense regime that Mrs Pumphrey herself could have followed if she had loved wisely. Herriot does not correct her — he just smiles.

**Character summary:**
- **Herriot** — practical, wise, kind, honest about his own weaknesses; a good vet who understands both animals and people. He avoids hurting Mrs Pumphrey's feelings but solves the problem.
- **Mrs Pumphrey** — rich, generous, affectionate, but foolish and over-indulgent; she learns (perhaps) that love needs discipline.
- **Tricki** — the innocent victim of too much love.

**Themes:** wise love vs blind love; discipline and health; irony and gentle humour; the bond between humans and pets.

check.q: Why is the title 'A Triumph of Surgery' ironic?
options: No surgery was done — only diet and exercise cured him
check.why: Mrs Pumphrey thinks a medical miracle happened, but the 'cure' was simple common sense with no operation.

parts.md: Bruno, a Labrador in a Chennai flat, had become the shape of a pillow. Grandma fed him idlis with ghee, Glucose biscuits at four, and a piece of every sweet from the Deepavali box. When he started panting on the stairs, the family vet, Dr Lakshmi, came home and listened to his heart. Then she noticed the biscuit tin by his bowl.

'He doesn't need medicine,' she said gently to Grandma. 'He needs walks on Besant Nagar beach and food in a measuring cup — and no chocolate ever; it's poisonous for dogs.' Grandma looked hurt, so Dr Lakshmi added, 'Your love is the medicine — just give it in walks instead of biscuits.' Six weeks later Bruno chased crows on the sand. Grandma told the neighbours the vet was a magician. Dr Lakshmi, like Herriot, simply smiled.

rd-school-c10-english-a.fp-triumph-surge.title: A Triumph of Surgery — Chapter Companion (part 2)
rd-school-c10-english-a.fp-triumph-surge.subtitle: Tricki's illness and cure scene by scene, the humour of the 'triumph', characters, themes and exam answers

sections.md:
James Herriot, a Yorkshire vet, tells this story in the first person. The patient is **Tricki**, a little Pekinese dog owned by the wealthy **Mrs Pumphrey**.

**1. A worrying sight.** Herriot sees Mrs Pumphrey walking Tricki on the street and is shocked. The dog is hugely fat, like a bloated sausage, with bloodshot eyes and a lolling tongue. Mrs Pumphrey explains he is listless and has no energy — and she has been giving him extra treats such as cream cakes and chocolates to build him up.

**2. Advice ignored.** Herriot tells her firmly to cut down his food, stop the sweets and give him more exercise. She agrees, but she cannot resist the dog's pleading eyes, and the household keeps spoiling him.

**3. Things get worse.** Tricki refuses food, vomits, lies on a rug panting and will not walk. Mrs Pumphrey phones in panic.

**4. The decision.** Herriot sees that the only cure is to take Tricki away from the home where he is spoilt. He says the dog must come to the surgery for about two weeks for observation. Mrs Pumphrey is close to fainting at the idea of parting with him.

**5. Arrival at the surgery.** Tricki arrives with luxuries — his own bed, cushions, toys, coats and plenty of food. Herriot's colleagues watch the scene with amusement.

**6. The 'treatment'.** For two days Tricki gets no food, only water. Then he begins to take an interest. He is put among the big surgery dogs, who run and play in the yard. Tricki joins them, competes for food at mealtimes, and slowly becomes slim, quick and lively.

**7. Gifts.** Mrs Pumphrey phones daily and sends fresh eggs and bottles of wine and brandy to help Tricki 'recover'. Herriot and his colleagues enjoy the gifts themselves, and Herriot jokes about how pleasant life at the surgery has become.

**8. The return.** After about a fortnight Mrs Pumphrey arrives in her chauffeur-driven car. Tricki leaps from Herriot's arms into her lap. She is overjoyed and calls the cure 'a triumph of surgery', thinking Herriot performed some brilliant feat. Herriot does not tell her that the cure was simply no sweets and lots of exercise.

check.q: What actually cured Tricki?
options: Strict diet and exercise with other dogs
check.why: Herriot only stopped the rich food and let Tricki play with the surgery dogs; no surgery was done.

sections.md:
A **triumph of surgery** suggests a dramatic operation by a brilliant surgeon. In fact no knife was ever used. The 'medicine' was common sense: a short fast, then a normal diet and plenty of running about. Mrs Pumphrey, who cannot imagine that her love was the cause of the illness, believes something wonderful must have been done. Herriot, a gentle man, lets her keep her belief.

The irony works on two levels:
- **Situational irony:** the cure is the opposite of what she thinks.
- **Comic irony:** the vets enjoy the rich gifts sent for the dog, while the dog grows thin on plain food.

sections.md:
**Mrs Pumphrey** — rich, kind-hearted, generous and loving, but foolish in her love. She treats Tricki like a spoilt child and cannot say no to him. She is not a villain; her fault is **over-indulgence**. She is also willing to trust the vet and truly grateful.

**James Herriot** — a sensible, humorous, kind professional. He diagnoses the real problem (over-feeding, no exercise) and acts firmly, yet he is tactful: he never insults Mrs Pumphrey. He is also honest with the reader about enjoying the gifts — this self-mocking touch makes the story warm.

**Tricki** — at first a lazy, sick lapdog; later a lively, normal dog. His change shows what a natural life can do.

**The surgery dogs and Herriot's colleagues** — they help, without knowing it, by giving Tricki company, competition and play.
keyTerms: over-indulgence — giving too much of what someone wants
listless — lacking energy
convalescence — the time of getting well

check.q: What is Mrs Pumphrey's main fault?
check.why: Her love leads her to over-feed and pamper Tricki, which makes him ill.

sections.md:
- **Love must be wise.** Pampering is not the same as caring. This applies to children too: too many sweets, screens and too little play can harm health.
- **Health through simple living.** A balanced diet and exercise cure what luxury caused.
- **Professional tact.** A good doctor treats both the patient and the worried owner.
- **Humour and gentle satire.** Herriot mocks the habits of the rich without cruelty.

**Did you know?** 'James Herriot' was the pen-name of Alf Wight, a real vet in Yorkshire, England. His books about country life as a vet became hugely popular and were adapted for television.

**Q. Why is Herriot concerned about Tricki? (about 60 words)** Tricki has become grossly fat, with bloodshot eyes and a hanging tongue. He refuses food, vomits and lies panting. Herriot realises this is caused by over-feeding with sweets and cream cakes and a lack of exercise, and that the dog's health is in real danger.

**Q. Why did Herriot take Tricki to the surgery?** To remove him from Mrs Pumphrey's pampering, which she could not stop on her own.

**Q. Is Herriot dishonest in accepting the gifts?** Discuss: he did not ask for them, the dog could not use them, and he admits it with humour — so most readers see it as light comedy. But you may argue he could have refused.

**Q. Would you call Mrs Pumphrey an ideal pet owner?** Loving yes, ideal no — explain.

**Exercise topics in the book:** Herriot's advice and why it was not followed; the treatment; Mrs Pumphrey's reaction; discussion on what makes a responsible pet owner; and whether wealthy people spoil their pets or children.

rd-school-c10-english-b.english-revision.subtitle: Every chapter of First Flight and Footprints, plus grammar and writing, in one sitting.

sections.h: How to Use This Revision Read
sections.md:
Two weeks before the board exam, nobody has time to reread two textbooks. This read compresses **First Flight** (prose and poetry) and **Footprints Without Feet** (supplementary reader), plus **grammar** and **writing**, into revision maps you can scan in about forty minutes.

For each chapter you get: **author · one-line gist · key characters · themes · one likely question**. Use it like this:

1. **Day 1–3**: read one block per day, then close the screen and explain each chapter aloud in 30 seconds.
2. **Day 4–6**: answer the 'likely question' for each chapter in 40 words (short) or 120 words (long).
3. **Day 7**: do the grammar and writing checks; time yourself on one full sample paper from your board.

Note: the syllabus is revised from time to time and some chapters may be deleted in a given year. **Check your school's current syllabus** before skipping anything.

> *Revision secret*: you remember what you *retrieve*, not what you *re-read*. Testing yourself beats highlighting.

check.q: According to memory research, which revision method works best?
check.why: Retrieval practice—recalling answers from memory—strengthens long-term memory more than re-reading or highlighting.

### Character quick-hits
- **Lencho** — hard-working, innocent, faithful, ungrateful to the humans who helped.
- **Valli** — curious, determined, mature for her age.
- **Lomov** — nervous, hypochondriac, argumentative.
- **Natalya** — quarrelsome but desperate to marry.
- **Chubukov** — self-interested father who wants Natalya married off.

| **The Ball Poem** | John Berryman | A boy loses a ball and learns the 'epistemology of loss'. |
| **Amanda!** | Robin Klein | A girl nagged by an adult escapes into daydreams of freedom. |
| **The Trees** | Adrienne Rich | Trees moving from house to forest; nature reclaiming freedom. |
| **Fog** | Carl Sandburg | Fog comes 'on little cat feet' — an extended metaphor. |
| **The Tale of Custard the Dragon** | Ogden Nash | A 'cowardly' dragon turns brave against a pirate; mock-heroic ballad. |
| **For Anne Gregory** | W. B. Yeats | Outer beauty vs inner worth. |

### Poetic devices you must name
- **Metaphor** — *Fog* is a cat. **Simile** — *as brave as a tiger*.
- **Personification** — trees that move; fog that sits.
- **Symbolism** — crow and hemlock (gloom) in *Dust of Snow*; fire and ice.
- **Alliteration** — repeated initial sounds.
- **Enjambment** — a sentence running over a line break.
- **Rhyme scheme** — e.g., *Dust of Snow* is *abab cdcd*.

**Likely long questions (120 words)**:
- *How did Ausable's presence of mind save him?*
- *Griffin was a brilliant scientist but a lawless man. Discuss.*
- *What lessons does 'The Necklace' teach about pride and honesty?*
- *How did education change Hari Singh?*

sections.md:
### Grammar checklist
1. **Tenses** — present perfect never with definite past time; past perfect for the earlier past action; *since* (point) / *for* (period).
2. **Modals** — base verb after modals; *must not* (forbidden) vs *need not* (not necessary).
3. **Concord** — find the head noun; *neither…nor* agrees with nearer subject; *each/every* singular.
4. **Determiners** — *a/an* by sound; *few/little* (hardly any) vs *a few/a little* (some).
5. **Reported speech** — pronoun, tense, time, place shift; questions use statement order.
6. **Editing/omission** — one error per line; scan Tense → Modal → Subject–verb → Determiner → Preposition.

### Writing checklist
| Task | Words | Must-haves |
|---|---|---|
| Formal letter | 100–120 | address, date, receiver, subject, salutation, 3 paras, closing |
| Analytical paragraph | 100–120 | intro, overview, details with numbers, conclusion |

### Answer-writing rules for literature
- **Short answer (40–50 words)**: answer in the first sentence, then one detail as evidence.
- **Long answer (100–120 words)**: claim → 2–3 pieces of evidence from the text → value/lesson.
- Use character names correctly; spell author names right.
- For extract-based questions, **read the lines twice** and answer from the extract.

check.q: Which is the best first sentence for a short literature answer?
options: A long introduction to the author
A direct answer to the question
check.why: Examiners reward short answers that state the answer immediately and then support it with a detail from the text.

sections.md:
### Time plan (3-hour paper — adapt to your board's latest pattern)
| Section | Suggested time |
|---|---|
| Reading (comprehension) | 40 min |
| Grammar | 20 min |
| Writing (letter + analytical paragraph) | 40 min |
| Literature | 65 min |
| Revision | 15 min |

### Exam-day habits
- Read the whole paper in the 15-minute reading time and **mark** the questions you're surest about.
- Write the **question number** clearly; leave a line between answers.
- Underline key words sparingly — not whole paragraphs.
- Never leave an MCQ blank; eliminate two options and choose wisely.
- Keep **word limits**: overlong answers waste time and seldom earn more.

### The night before
Sleep at least 7–8 hours. Sleep consolidates memory; late-night cramming usually lowers next-day recall. Pack your admit card, pens and water bottle before dinner.

> *Did you know?* Studies on 'spacing' show that revising a topic on three separate days beats revising it three times in one day — same effort, better memory.

sections.h: Value points: one long answer per prose chapter
sections.md:
For each chapter, here are the **three points** a 120-word answer should contain. Learn the points, not paragraphs.

| Chapter | Likely long question | Three value points |
|---|---|---|
| A Letter to God | Faith vs. human kindness | Lencho's total faith; postmaster's kindness and collection; irony of Lencho blaming the helpers |
| Long Walk to Freedom | Meaning of courage | Courage is triumph over fear; oppressor and oppressed both need liberation; twin obligations |
| From the Diary of Anne Frank | Why write a diary? | Lonely and in need of a true friend; diary 'Kitty' as confidant; humour in the Mr Keesing episode |
| Glimpses of India | Culture and region | Goan baker tradition; Coorg's people and coffee country; Assam tea legends and estates |
| Mijbil the Otter | Bond between man and animal | Maxwell's care; otter's playfulness; difficulties of travel and the box episode |
| Madam Rides the Bus | Valli's growing up | Planning and saving; confident behaviour on the bus; the dead cow brings awareness of death |
| The Sermon at Benares | Universality of death | Kisa Gotami's grief; mustard seed from a house with no death; acceptance and wisdom |
| The Proposal | Satire on marriage | Practical reasons for the match; quarrels over land and dogs; ironic ending |

For Footprints: Triumph of Surgery (wise love), Thief's Story (trust reforms), Midnight Visitor (wit beats force), A Question of Trust (the cheater cheated), Footprints without Feet (science without ethics), Making of a Scientist (curiosity and mentoring), The Necklace (pride and appearance), Bholi (education gives voice), Book that Saved the Earth (value of books, humour of misreading).

A mustard seed from a house where no one has died

**How to answer a device question:** name the device → point to the line → say what effect it creates. Example: 'In *Fog*, the fog is compared to a cat moving on little feet. This metaphor shows how silently and gently fog arrives.'

(Syllabus lists change by year: check which poems your board currently prescribes.)
keyTerms: extended metaphor — a comparison carried through a whole poem
mock-heroic — treating a silly subject in a grand style

sections.md:
Grammar questions test a handful of rules again and again. Use the **clue word** method: find the word in the sentence that decides the answer.

- **since / for / already / yet / just** → present perfect (has/have + past participle).
- **yesterday / ago / in 2019 / last week** → simple past, never present perfect.
- **by the time / before / after** with two past actions → past perfect for the earlier one.
- **neither…nor / either…or** → verb agrees with the nearer subject.
- **each / every / one of / neither of** → singular verb.
- **a / an** goes by sound: an hour, a university, an MLA.
- **few / little** = hardly any (negative); **a few / a little** = some (positive). Few with countable nouns, little with uncountable.
- **Modals** are followed by the base verb: can go, must finish, should have gone.

The worked examples at the end of this part show four common question types step by step.

check.q: Choose the correct form: 'She ___ in Pune since 2019.'
check.why: 'Since' with a point in time that continues to now needs the present perfect: has lived.

sections.md:
Unseen passages carry many marks. Use a four-step routine:

1. **Skim (1 minute).** Read the title, first and last paragraph. Ask: what is the main idea?
2. **Read questions first.** Underline key words in each question.
3. **Scan for answers.** Find the paragraph; the answer is usually within one or two sentences.
4. **Vocabulary questions.** Replace the word with each option and see which keeps the meaning.

For **case-based / factual passages** with tables or figures, look at units and dates carefully; many wrong answers come from reading the wrong row.

**Inference questions** ('What does the writer suggest…') need you to think one step beyond the words. Support your inference with one clue from the passage.

check.q: What should you do first in an unseen passage?
check.why: Skimming gives the overall idea, which makes every later question faster.

sections.md:
**Task:** Write a letter to the editor of a newspaper about plastic waste on the beach in your city.

- **Sender's address** (Flat 12, Sea View Road, Chennai) and **date**
- **Receiver:** The Editor, *The Daily Herald*, Chennai
- **Subject:** Plastic litter on Marina Beach
- **Salutation:** Sir/Madam,
- **Para 1 — purpose:** Through your esteemed newspaper I wish to draw attention to…
- **Para 2 — details:** bottles and wrappers after weekends and festivals; harm to fish, turtles and tourism.
- **Para 3 — suggestions:** more bins, fines, school clean-up drives, no single-use plastic at stalls.
- **Closing:** Yours faithfully, name.

**Analytical paragraph tip:** begin with what the chart shows (topic, time span), give the overall trend, then two or three key comparisons with numbers, and end with a one-line conclusion. Never invent reasons the data does not support — say 'this may be due to…'.

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-bholi.title: Bholi — A Complete Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-bholi.subtitle: How a girl everyone called 'simpleton' found her voice — and used it to say no.

sections.h: A Hook: The Girl Who Could Not Speak
sections.md:
Imagine being seven years old and dreading every question anyone asks you, because the moment you open your mouth the words get stuck, and the room fills with laughter. Now imagine that, twenty years later, you stand in front of a wedding crowd, a garland in your hand, and you speak so clearly that the whole village goes silent.

That is the arc of **Bholi**, a short story by **Khwaja Ahmad Abbas** (K. A. Abbas, 1914–1987) — journalist, novelist, screenwriter and film director, best known for socially conscious cinema. In this chapter of *Footprints Without Feet*, Abbas uses one girl's life to ask a hard question about Indian villages of his time: **what happens to a girl whom no one thinks is worth educating?**

The story moves in clear stages:

1. A childhood accident and illness that leave Bholi slow of speech and pock-marked.
2. Neglect at home — because she is 'plain' and 'not quite right', no one expects her to marry.
3. A government girls' school opens; Bholi is sent there *only* because she seems unmarriageable.
4. A kind teacher gives her confidence and the gift of speech and reading.
5. A marriage is fixed with an old, lame, greedy grocer, Bishamber Nath.
6. At the wedding, Bishamber demands dowry; Bholi's father pays and is humiliated.
7. Bholi refuses to marry him — and announces she will serve her parents and teach in the school.

Keep this ladder in mind. Every exam question about Bholi is really asking you about one of these rungs.

> *Did you know?* K. A. Abbas wrote the story for the film *Awara* (1951) and directed *Saat Hindustani* (1969), the first film of Amitabh Bachchan.
keyTerms: Simpleton — a person thought to be foolish or slow; the meaning of 'Bholi'
Dowry — money or goods demanded from a bride's family at marriage; illegal in India under the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961

check.q: Why was Bholi finally sent to school?
options: Her father believed strongly in girls' education
The Tehsildar had to set an example, and Bholi seemed unlikely to marry anyway
check.why: Ramlal had to send a daughter to set an example for the Tehsildar's new school, and the family chose Bholi because they felt her plainness made marriage unlikely, so schooling cost them nothing.

sections.h: Childhood: The Fall and the Fever
sections.md:
Bholi's real name is **Sulekha**. She is the fourth daughter of **Ramlal**, the *numberdar* (village headman) of a village. Her name 'Bholi' — *simpleton* — sticks to her because of two misfortunes.

**The fall.** When she was ten months old, she fell off a cot (in the story, she slips off and hurts her head). A part of her brain was perhaps damaged, the narrator suggests, and she remained a backward child.

**The smallpox.** At two, she suffered smallpox. She survived, but deep black pock-marks covered her face and body. Until five she could not speak; when she did, she **stammered**. Other children mocked her by mimicking her speech, so she spoke less and less.

Notice how Abbas places her within the family. Ramlal has seven children — three sons and four daughters — and the youngest of them is a son. Ramlal is well-off; the family has enough to eat. But it is not poverty that hurts Bholi. It is **attitude**. Her brothers and sisters are healthy and good-looking; she is the one nobody quite knows what to do with. She wears old, cast-off clothes; she is given the least attention.

### Why these details matter
Abbas wants you to see that Bholi's 'problem' is partly physical and partly **made by others**. A stammer is made worse by mockery. Shyness is made worse by neglect. The story is asking you to separate what nature did to her from what society did to her.

> *Did you know?* Smallpox was declared eradicated from India in 1977 and from the world in 1980 — one of the great public-health victories of the 20th century.

sections.h: The School Comes to the Village
sections.md:
A turning point arrives with a new official. The **Tehsildar** comes to open a **primary school for girls** in the village and tells Ramlal that, as a government official and numberdar, he must set an example by sending his daughters.

At home, Ramlal's wife objects: if girls go to school, who will marry them? The conversation is coldly practical. The older daughters are already married or about to be; the next, **Mangala**, is marriageable. Then they think of Bholi. She is plain, pock-marked and 'not quite right'. Nobody will marry her, so sending *her* to school costs nothing. **This is the irony at the heart of the story: Bholi is sent to school because she is considered worthless.**

### Bholi's first day
Bholi is bathed, her hair oiled, and given a clean dress — things that almost never happened to her. She thinks of the cow, Lakshmi, being washed and decorated before being sold at the fair; she half fears she is being sent away too. On the way she clings to her father's hand.

At school she sees **many girls her own age** and, for the first time, a world that is bright, with pictures and colours on the walls. Then the teacher asks her name. She stammers. The other girls laugh. She weeps.

And then something new happens. The **teacher** does not laugh. She speaks softly, pats her, and says Bholi should try once more, slowly, and she *will* be able to say it. Bholi manages: 'Bh-Bh-Bholi'. The teacher praises her and promises that if she comes regularly she will speak like everyone else.

> *Did you know?* Abbas wrote this story when female literacy in India was very low. In the 1951 Census it was under 9%; by the 2011 Census it was about 65%.

right.title: School
points: Clean clothes, oiled hair on day one
Told she can learn and speak

check.q: What did Bholi think of when she was bathed and dressed for school?
options: The cow Lakshmi being washed before being sold
check.why: Bholi remembered the cow Lakshmi being washed and decorated before being taken to the fair to be sold, and feared she too was being sent away.

sections.md:
The teacher is never named, which tells you something: she stands for **what education can do**. Look closely at her method; examiners love this question.

- **Patience** — she lets Bholi try again rather than finishing the word for her.
- **Affection** — she pats her, speaks softly, and Bholi feels her kindness as 'the voice of love'.
- **Encouragement** — she promises a future: 'come every day, and you will speak like everyone else'.
- **A gift** — she hands Bholi a colourful **picture book**, saying that soon she will read it, and then she will be respected and 'no one will dare to laugh at you'.
- **Dignity** — she tells her she will become the most learned person in the village.

The narrator says that Bholi's heart began to fill with a new hope, a new life. Notice the vocabulary: Abbas does not show Bholi changing overnight. Years pass. She goes to school, learns to read and write, and slowly her stammer fades. By the time the next crisis arrives, she is a confident young woman — although her family still sees her as 'Bholi'.

### Why the teacher matters to the theme
The teacher shows that **disability and plainness are not destiny**. A child who is told she is a burden behaves like one; a child who is told she can learn begins to learn. This is the chapter's quiet argument for girls' education and for compassionate teaching.

> *Did you know?* Speech therapists today say the same thing the teacher sensed: for many children who stammer, patience, slow speech and freedom from mockery help more than anything else.
keyTerms: Compassion — kindness that comes from understanding another's pain
Self-confidence — trust in one's own ability

check.q: What did the teacher give Bholi on her first day?
check.why: The teacher gave Bholi a colourful picture book and promised she would soon read it and be respected by everyone.

sections.md:
Years later, a proposal arrives for Bholi from **Bishamber Nath**, a well-to-do **grocer** from a nearby village. On paper he seems a 'catch' for a family that has given up on Bholi. But consider the facts Abbas lays out:

- He is **old** — around fifty; he has a grown-up family from his first marriage.
- He **limps**; he is lame.
- He has a shop and money — and, it turns out, greed.
- He **does not ask for a dowry** at first, which Ramlal's wife sees as a blessing: 'Bholi is lucky.'

Ramlal hesitates because of the age gap, but his wife argues that a plain, half-wit girl cannot expect better, and that Bishamber's good fortune and absence of dowry demand make it a sensible match. Bholi is not asked. Her silence is assumed to be agreement. This is the same family logic that sent her to school: **she is treated as an object to be disposed of conveniently.**

### The wedding day
The wedding is fixed and preparations begin. The groom arrives with a band, in procession. The women of the family dress Bholi in red silk, with a veil; but under the veil she is silent and thoughtful, and nobody imagines she has opinions.

At the moment of the garland exchange (*the jaimala*), Bishamber pushes aside Bholi's veil and sees her pock-marked face for the first time. He pulls Ramlal aside and **demands five thousand rupees** as dowry, or he will take the procession back.

> *Did you know?* Dowry has been a punishable offence in India since the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 — yet stories like this one remind us why the law was needed.

check.q: How much dowry did Bishamber demand at the wedding?
check.why: On seeing Bholi's face, Bishamber demanded five thousand rupees as dowry, threatening to return without marrying her.

sections.md:
Ramlal is stunned. He pleads, puts his **turban at Bishamber's feet** — a public act of great humiliation — and begs him not to dishonour the family. Bishamber is unmoved. Ramlal brings out the money and counts five thousand rupees into the groom's hands.

The groom, satisfied, reaches out to place the garland on the bride. And then — the moment the whole story has been building towards — **Bholi throws the garland into the fire** (in the story she flings it away) and pushes off her veil.

She speaks — clearly, without a stammer — to her father: she will **not marry** this mean, greedy, contemptible man. Take back the money, she says. The crowd is astonished: 'Bholi can speak!' Bishamber, shamed, leaves with his party. The villagers whisper; the guests drift away.

Ramlal, crushed, worries aloud that **now no one will ever marry her**. Bholi answers calmly: she will look after him and her mother in their old age and **teach in the same school** where she learned. She is not afraid.

The story closes with the teacher in the shadows — she has watched it all — feeling the quiet satisfaction of an artist who sees her masterpiece complete.

### What changed?
The stammer that defined her childhood is gone, but more importantly the **silence** is gone. She has learned not only to speak, but to speak *up*. Education gave her words; self-respect gave her the courage to use them.

| Character | Who | Key traits | Role in theme |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bholi (Sulekha)** | Ramlal's fourth daughter | Neglected, stammering, slow → confident, articulate, self-respecting | Shows the power of education and courage |
| **Ramlal** | Numberdar, her father | Well-meaning but weak; ruled by social pressure; loving at the end | Represents a father trapped by custom |
| **Ramlal's wife** | Her mother | Practical, worried about marriage, dismissive of Bholi | Voices society's view of girls as a burden |
| **The teacher** | Unnamed schoolteacher | Kind, patient, encouraging | The transforming force of compassionate education |
| **Bishamber Nath** | Grocer, ~50, lame | Greedy, mean, opportunistic | Embodies the evil of dowry |
| **Tehsildar** | Government official | Progressive | Brings the school — the state's role in change |

### Character sketch of Bholi (exam-ready, 120 words)
Bholi is the neglected fourth daughter of Ramlal. A fall in infancy and smallpox at two leave her slow, stammering and scarred; her family treats her as a burden and dresses her in cast-offs. Sent to school only because she seems unmarriageable, she meets a gentle teacher whose patience and affection unlock her speech and her self-belief. Years of learning turn her into a thoughtful, articulate young woman. Her finest moment comes at her wedding: when the old, greedy Bishamber demands dowry and humiliates her father, she flings away the garland and refuses him. She chooses dignity over a marriage of shame, promising to serve her parents and teach. She is proof that education creates courage.

check.q: Which character best represents the social evil the story attacks?
check.why: Bishamber Nath, who demands dowry after seeing Bholi's face, embodies the greed and contempt for women that the dowry system expresses.

sections.md:
**1. The transforming power of education.** Bholi's change is not magic; it is schooling plus a teacher who believes in her. Education gives her literacy, speech and, most of all, a sense of her own worth.

**2. Gender discrimination.** Daughters are measured by beauty and marriageability. Bholi is sent to school because she is 'useless' for marriage — a bitter irony. Her mother's words show how women themselves can carry these attitudes.

**3. The evil of dowry.** Bishamber's demand is shown as shameful and humiliating, and Bholi's refusal as heroic. The story was written to change minds.

**4. Compassion versus mockery.** Laughter silenced Bholi; kindness gave her a voice. The story is a lesson in how we treat anyone who is 'different' — a child who stammers, a child with a disability.

**5. Self-respect and courage.** Bholi prefers being unmarried to being married with dishonour. In the 1950s–60s village, this was a radical choice.

### Symbols
- **The cow Lakshmi** — Bholi's fear of being 'sold' like an animal; it foreshadows her treatment as property in the marriage.
- **The picture book** — the promise of learning and respect.
- **The garland and fire** — the moment she rejects a ritual that would have bound her to humiliation.
- **The stammer** — her silence; its disappearance marks her inner freedom.

### Title
'Bholi' is ironic. The girl called simpleton turns out to be the only person at the wedding with the clarity to see what is right.

check.q: What does the cow Lakshmi symbolise in the story?
options: Bholi's fear of being treated as property and sent away
check.why: Bholi's memory of Lakshmi being washed before sale reflects her fear—and the reality—of girls being handed over like property.

sections.md:
### Useful vocabulary
- **numberdar** — village headman responsible for land revenue records
- **tehsildar** — revenue officer of a tehsil (sub-district)
- **pock-marks** — scars left by smallpox
- **procession / baraat** — groom's party arriving for a wedding
- **dowry** — illegal demand of money or goods at marriage
- **contemptible** — deserving to be looked down on

### How to answer the value-based question
CBSE often asks a 100–120 word value question, e.g. *'Bholi's teacher played a crucial role in her life. Discuss.'* Use this structure:
1. **Claim** — the teacher transformed Bholi from a silent, frightened child into a confident woman.
2. **Evidence** — gentle tone, no mockery, asked her to try again, gave a picture book, promised respect.
3. **Effect** — Bholi learned to read and speak; years later she rejected Bishamber.
4. **Value** — good teachers build self-esteem; education is the key to women's empowerment.

### Diary entry / letter tasks
You may be asked to write Bholi's diary on her first day at school, or her letter to her teacher after the wedding. Write in first person, past tense, with feelings (fear, wonder, gratitude) and specific details from the story — the colours on the walls, the girls laughing, the teacher's touch.

### Common mistakes
- Writing that Bishamber demanded dowry *before* the wedding — he demanded it **at** the wedding, after seeing her face.
- Calling the teacher Bholi's relative — she is an unnamed schoolteacher.
- Saying Bholi married someone else — she chose not to marry and to teach.
keyTerms: Irony — a contrast between what is expected and what happens
Foreshadowing — an early hint of a later event

sections.h: The teacher: why she changes everything
sections.md:
K. A. Abbas gives Bholi's teacher only a few scenes, yet she is the hinge of the story. Look at what she does:

- **Gentle voice.** Bholi has only ever heard scolding. The teacher speaks softly, so Bholi stops trembling.
- **A colourful picture book.** She promises Bholi bigger books and says she will become the most learned person in the village. Books become a symbol of a new life.
- **Patience with the stammer.** She lets Bholi say her name slowly and tells her that if she speaks without fear, the stammer will go.
- **Respect.** She treats Bholi as a person with a future, not as a burden.

Years later, when Bholi refuses to marry the greedy Bishamber, she speaks clearly and firmly — the teacher's lesson has borne fruit. At the end the teacher is described as feeling the pride of an artist who sees her work completed. The message: one caring teacher can transform a neglected child.

check.q: What does the teacher promise Bholi on the first day?
options: That she will become the most learned person in the village
check.why: The teacher encourages her with books and the promise that learning will make her respected.

sections.md:
**Symbols**
- **The name 'Bholi'** (simpleton) versus her real name **Sulekha** (one who writes well) — the story moves her from the first to the second.
- **New clothes** on the school day: for once she is treated with care, but they come only because the family wants to be rid of her.
- **The garland** Bholi throws away: rejection of a marriage based on dowry and insult.

**Social issues raised** (useful for long answers)
1. **Neglect of girl children** — Bholi was left uncared for after an illness and a fall.
2. **Dowry** — Bishamber demands five thousand rupees after seeing her pock-marked face.
3. **Education of girls** — the Tehsildar's push opens a school for girls; education gives Bholi a voice.
4. **Old age and marriage** — her parents accept an older, lame groom because they think no one else will marry her.

**Did you know?** K. A. Abbas was also a noted filmmaker and screenwriter; many of his stories argue for social reform.

**Q. 'Bholi's teacher played a significant role in changing the course of her life.' Discuss. (120 words)**
Bholi was a neglected, stammering girl whom her family thought dull. On her first day at school the teacher spoke to her kindly, showed her a picture book and promised that learning would make her respected in the village. She told Bholi to speak without fear, and Bholi slowly gained confidence. Education gave her the courage to think for herself. So when the old, greedy Bishamber demanded dowry at her wedding, Bholi rejected him publicly and chose to stay with her parents and teach at the school. The teacher turned a frightened child into a confident young woman, showing how compassion and education can change a life.

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-book-saved-ea.title: The Book That Saved the Earth — A Complete Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-book-saved-ea.subtitle: Martians, a library, a bossy genius and a book of nursery rhymes. Guess who wins.

sections.h: A Hook: How Can a Children's Book Stop an Invasion?
sections.md:
Picture a fleet of spaceships from Mars, ready to conquer Earth. The commanders are clever, the weapons are advanced, the plan is perfect. And what stops them? Not a missile. Not a superhero. A **book of nursery rhymes** — *Mother Goose* — read by the wrong people in the wrong way.

**The Book That Saved the Earth** is a short science-fiction **comedy play** by the American writer **Claire Boiko**, known for plays written for young performers. It appears in *Footprints Without Feet*, and it is the only full play in that book — which means you must read it as drama: characters, stage directions, dialogue, dramatic irony and a twist ending.

### The frame
The play is set in the future and told by a **Historian** speaking from the **twenty-fifth century**. She (or he — the part can be played by anyone) looks back at a famous episode: the Martian attempt to invade Earth in the **twenty-first century**. Her job is to explain to the audience why, of all things, *a book* is honoured as Earth's saviour.

This frame gives the play two layers of humour:
1. **We know what the Martians don't.** We recognise the nursery rhymes instantly; the Martians take them as secret military information.
2. **The future looks back at us.** The Historian talks about books as if they were half-forgotten wonders, which gently asks: *are we forgetting how to read?*

> *Did you know?* Mother Goose rhymes like 'Hey Diddle Diddle' and 'Humpty Dumpty' were in print in England by the 18th–19th centuries, and many are far older as oral rhymes.

check.q: From which century does the Historian narrate the story?
check.why: The Historian speaks from the twenty-fifth century and looks back at the Martian attempt on Earth in the twenty-first century.

sections.md:
| Character | Who | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| **Historian** | Narrator from the 25th century | Frames the story; explains the 'Age of the Book' in hindsight |
| **Think-Tank** | Great and mighty ruler of Mars | Huge, egg-shaped head; boastful, arrogant, rude; insists he is the most brilliant being in the universe; insults everyone |
| **Noodle** | Think-Tank's apprentice | Humble, clever, quick; keeps finding ways to correct his master without offending him |
| **Captain Omega** | Commander of the Martian probe | Obedient, nervous, follows orders |
| **Lieutenant Iota** | Crew member | Disciplined; reads aloud on order |
| **Sergeant Oop** | Crew member | Bumbling, fearful; tastes and treats a book like food |

### Think-Tank, the comic centre
Think-Tank is a classic **'pompous fool'**. He calls himself 'Great and Mighty Think-Tank, Commander-in-Chief of Mars', demands to be addressed with long titles and calls his subordinates names like *'stupid'* and *'idiot'*. He is certain of everything and right about almost nothing. His mistakes drive the whole plot.

And Noodle? Noodle is the quiet hero inside the joke. Every time Think-Tank wants to change his mind without looking foolish, Noodle offers a 'suggestion' that lets the boss save face. You'll meet this pattern again and again: **Think-Tank is wrong → Noodle politely suggests the truth → Think-Tank claims the idea as his own.**

sections.md:
### The Historian's prologue
The Historian begins by explaining that the twenty-first century was a time when books were valued and loved, and invites us to see the strange story of how a book rescued the planet. The play then 'cuts' to Mars Space Control.

### Mars Space Control
Think-Tank sits at the centre, surrounded by screens, and Noodle stands by. Think-Tank boasts about his intellect. The Martian probe ship — Captain Omega, Lieutenant Iota and Sergeant Oop — has landed on Earth at a place called **Centerville**, inside a building that turns out to be a **public library**.

Think-Tank orders a report. Omega describes a strange building full of objects arranged on shelves. Think-Tank decides at once what they must be: **sandwiches**! (He is certain Earthlings store food on shelves.) The crew obediently try to eat a book. Oop chews a page and finds it dry and tasteless.

Noodle tactfully offers another idea: perhaps these objects are **communication devices**. Think-Tank instantly adopts this as his own brilliant thought: of course! Earthlings *communicate* with these 'sandwiches'. The crew must 'listen' to the books — they hold them to their ears — and hear nothing.

Noodle suggests, very politely, that perhaps you must **look** at them — the marks may be a kind of code. Think-Tank orders the crew to use the 'Mars-to-Earth language translator' — and finally the books begin to make 'sense'.

### Why this scene is funny
Each step is a reversal: the most 'intelligent' being in the universe cannot work out what a library is, while the lowly apprentice keeps getting it right. The audience laughs because they know the answer from the first line.

check.q: What did Think-Tank first believe the books were?
check.why: Think-Tank arrogantly declared the books were sandwiches, and the crew even tried to eat them.

sections.md:
With the translator on, the crew read from a picture book of **Mother Goose rhymes**. Think-Tank interprets each one as top-secret military intelligence.

### 'Hey Diddle Diddle'
One rhyme tells of a cow that jumped over the moon. Think-Tank panics: if even Earth's **cows** have mastered space travel, how advanced must the **humans** be? The Martians had been planning to invade the Moon and use it as a base; now the Earthlings seem already to have the Moon covered — by cattle.

### 'Humpty Dumpty'
Then comes the picture that destroys Think-Tank's nerve: a large, **egg-shaped** figure sitting on a wall — and the rhyme says he had a great fall and could not be put back together again.

The egg looks exactly like **Think-Tank himself** (his giant head is famously egg-like). Think-Tank decides the book is a **warning** and a **plot**: Earthlings know about him and plan to make him fall. His arrogance turns to terror.

### The retreat
Think-Tank orders the probe ship to return at once, cancels the invasion and announces that the Martians will **evacuate** — he wants to flee to a distant, safe place (he names far-off Alpha Centauri in his panic). Noodle is left almost alone; the Historian returns to close the play.

### What the rhymes mean in the play
The joke is that **reading words is not the same as understanding them.** Think-Tank can decode letters but not **context, imagination or fun**. He reads fantasy as fact.

> *Did you know?* 'Humpty Dumpty' began life as a riddle — the answer was 'an egg' — which is why illustrators draw him as one.

sections.h: The Ending and the Historian's Message
sections.md:
The Historian steps forward to conclude: the Martians never came back, and that is why, she says, the book of nursery rhymes is remembered as **'the book that saved the Earth.'** The play also hints that relations improved over time — the Historian's tone is warm rather than triumphant.

Notice how the ending turns everything upside down:
- The **weakest**-looking object (a children's book) defeats the **strongest** empire.
- The **cleverest** character (Think-Tank) is the most **foolish**.
- The **humblest** character (Noodle) is the most **sensible**.

### Themes
1. **Arrogance leads to downfall.** Think-Tank refuses to listen, so he misreads everything. Pride blinds intelligence.
2. **Knowledge vs. wisdom.** Decoding words isn't understanding. True intelligence includes humility, imagination and context.
3. **The value of books.** Even 'silly' books carry a culture's imagination. A civilisation that reads, the play jokes, is hard to conquer.
4. **Misunderstanding across cultures.** The Martians judge Earth by their own assumptions — a gentle comment on how we misjudge strangers.
5. **Respect for the humble.** Noodle's tact shows how good ideas can come from anyone.

### Dramatic devices
- **Dramatic irony** — the audience knows more than the characters.
- **Frame narrative** — the Historian's prologue and epilogue.
- **Slapstick** — Oop tasting the book, the crew listening to pages.
- **Satire** — mocking pompous leaders who demand titles and praise.
keyTerms: Dramatic irony — when the audience understands something the characters do not
Satire — humour used to criticise foolishness or vice
Frame narrative — a story told inside another story

check.q: Which device makes the audience laugh when Think-Tank misreads the rhymes?
check.why: The audience knows the rhymes are harmless, but Think-Tank thinks they are military secrets, which is dramatic irony.

sections.md:
### Think-Tank (120 words)
Think-Tank is the self-proclaimed 'Great and Mighty' ruler of Mars, with an enormous egg-shaped head of which he is very proud. He is boastful, rude and impatient, insults his subordinates and demands flattering titles. He believes he cannot be wrong, so he declares books to be sandwiches and nursery rhymes to be secret codes. Yet he is also insecure: he quietly adopts Noodle's suggestions as his own to protect his image. When he sees Humpty Dumpty, his arrogance collapses into fear and he abandons the invasion. He embodies how pride and a closed mind can make even a brilliant brain foolish.

### Noodle (100 words)
Noodle is Think-Tank's small apprentice and the real brain of Mars Space Control. Humble and tactful, he never openly contradicts his master; instead he offers gentle 'suggestions' — books may be communication devices; perhaps they must be looked at, not listened to; perhaps a dictionary will help. He lets Think-Tank take the credit. His patience and practical sense show the value of wisdom over vanity, and of diplomacy in dealing with difficult bosses.

### Captain Omega, Iota and Oop
The crew follow orders without question. Oop is the comic figure — scared, clumsy, chewing a page. Through them the play laughs at blind obedience.

### Writing tip
For 'character' questions, give **3 traits + 1 incident each + what the character teaches us**.

check.q: Which quality best describes Noodle?
check.why: Noodle tactfully guides Think-Tank toward correct ideas without offending him, showing wisdom and diplomacy.

sections.h: Performing the Play and Answering Questions
sections.md:
Because it is a play, you may be asked to **stage** it or to write from a character's point of view.

### Staging notes
- **Two spaces**: Mars Space Control (screens, a big chair for Think-Tank) and the Centerville library (shelves of books).
- **Costume**: a giant egg-shaped head for Think-Tank — the visual joke that pays off with Humpty Dumpty.
- **Timing**: pause before each misreading so the audience can laugh *first*.

### Sample answers
**Q. Why did Think-Tank decide to abandon the invasion?** (40 words)
After hearing that even cows on Earth could jump over the moon, and seeing Humpty Dumpty — an egg-shaped figure like himself — fall off a wall, Think-Tank thought Earthlings were super-advanced and planned his downfall, so he fled in fear.

**Q. How is the play a satire on arrogance?** (120 words)
Structure: define arrogance → Think-Tank's titles and insults → misjudgements (sandwiches, listening) → stolen ideas from Noodle → panic at Humpty Dumpty → lesson: the proud mind cannot learn.

### Common mistakes
- Writing that the Martians *reached* Mars' moon plan — they wanted to use **Earth's** Moon/Earth; keep it general.
- Mixing up Noodle (apprentice) with Oop (sergeant).
- Forgetting the Historian's role in the frame.
keyTerms: Prologue — the opening speech before the action
Epilogue — the closing speech after the action

summary: Play by Claire Boiko; a science-fiction comedy in Footprints Without Feet.

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-book-saved-ea.title: The Book That Saved the Earth — A Complete Chapter Companion (part 2)
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-book-saved-ea.subtitle: Scene-by-scene retelling of the Martian invasion, the comedy of Mother Goose, characters and exam answers

sections.md:
Claire Boiko's short play is set in the future and looks back on the twentieth century. Here is every movement of the play in our own words.

**Prologue — the Historian.** A historian of the twenty-fifth century speaks to the audience. He explains that the twentieth century was once called the 'Era of the Book', when people read books on every subject. He promises to tell how a single book saved the Earth from a Martian invasion planned for the year 2040.

**Mars Space Control.** **Think-Tank**, the ruler of Mars, believes he is the most brilliant being in the universe and demands that his servants address him with grand titles. His enormous head is compared to a huge melon. His apprentice **Noodle** flatters him nervously. Think-Tank has sent a probe team to Earth to prepare for an invasion.

**The probe reaches Earth.** **Captain Omega**, **Lieutenant Iota** and **Sergeant Oop** land in a public library in a small American town. They find many books but do not know what books are. They decide the books must be sandwiches, and Oop tries to eat one. Think-Tank, watching on a screen, declares from his 'great wisdom' that they must be communication devices.

**Reading Mother Goose.** Noodle timidly suggests books may be meant for reading. Think-Tank takes the idea as his own and orders the team to open a book called *Mother Goose*. Omega and Iota read nursery rhymes aloud, and Think-Tank interprets each one in alarming ways:
- 'Hey diddle diddle, the cow jumped over the moon' → Earth must be so advanced that even its cows travel in space.
- 'Humpty Dumpty' → he notices that the egg-shaped figure looks like himself and fears the rhyme predicts his own great fall.
- 'Mistress Mary, quite contrary', with her strange garden → he reads it as a secret code about something dangerous on Earth.

**Panic and retreat.** Convinced that Earth is a super-civilisation and that he himself is in danger, Think-Tank calls off the invasion and orders a hasty retreat from Earth. Noodle is left behind to sort things out.

**Epilogue — the Historian returns.** He explains that, thanks to a book of nursery rhymes, the Earth was saved, and that later relations with Mars became friendly, with Noodle playing a peaceful part.

check.q: What does Think-Tank conclude from 'the cow jumped over the moon'?
check.why: He misreads the rhyme literally and decides Earth must be so advanced that even its animals fly to the moon.

sections.h: Why it is funny: misunderstanding as comedy
sections.md:
The humour depends on **dramatic irony** — the audience knows Mother Goose is a children's book; the 'genius' Think-Tank does not.

| Martian belief | Reality |
|---|---|
| Books are sandwiches | Books are for reading |
| Books are communication devices | They are printed pages |
| Rhymes are coded messages | They are nonsense verses for children |
| Earth is too powerful to attack | Earth knows nothing of the plan |

Think-Tank's **arrogance** is the real cause of his defeat. He brushes aside Noodle's sensible suggestions, or steals them, and takes credit for every 'brilliant' guess. Pride blinds him.

sections.md:
**Think-Tank** — vain, boastful, self-declared genius, easily frightened; his big head is a symbol of his inflated ego.

**Noodle** — humble, polite, sensible; he makes the right guesses (books are for reading) but is ignored or robbed of credit. He represents true intelligence that does not shout.

**Captain Omega** — the obedient leader of the probe; **Lieutenant Iota** — eager and loyal; **Sergeant Oop** — clumsy and comic.

**The Historian** — the narrator who frames the play and reminds us of the value of books.
keyTerms: probe — an exploratory mission
prologue / epilogue — speeches before and after a play
arrogance — exaggerated pride

check.why: Noodle suggests books are for reading, but Think-Tank dismisses him or claims the idea as his own.

sections.md:
- **Value of books and reading** — even a children's book proves powerful.
- **Pride goes before a fall** — Think-Tank's ego makes him run away.
- **Real intelligence is humble** — Noodle.
- **Humour and imagination** — science fiction used to make a point.

**Q. How did Mother Goose save the Earth? (100–120 words)**
Think-Tank sent a probe to Earth to prepare for an invasion. The Martians landed in a library and, not knowing what books were, opened Mother Goose. Think-Tank interpreted the nursery rhymes literally: a cow jumping over the moon meant Earth's animals could travel in space; Humpty Dumpty, who looked like him, seemed to warn of his own downfall; Mary's garden sounded like a hidden danger. Concluding that Earth was far too advanced, he cancelled the invasion and fled. So a simple book of rhymes, misread by an arrogant ruler, saved the Earth.

**Exercise topics:** Think-Tank's mistakes; Noodle's role; the meaning of the title; acting the play with sound effects.

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-footprints-wi.title: Footprints without Feet — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-footprints-wi.subtitle: Muddy footprints appear on a London street — but nobody is there. H. G. Wells's invisible scientist, explained

sections.md:
Two boys in a London square stop and stare. On the steps of a house, **fresh muddy footprints** are appearing, one after another — *as if someone were walking* — yet there is **no one there**. The boys follow the prints down the street until they grow fainter and vanish.

This eerie scene opens *Footprints without Feet*, adapted from **The Invisible Man** (1897) by **H. G. Wells** (1866–1946), the English writer often called a father of **science fiction**. Wells also wrote *The Time Machine* and *The War of the Worlds*.

The chapter follows **Griffin**, a brilliant scientist who discovers how to make the human body **invisible**. But invisibility doesn't make him happy or powerful — it makes him **lawless, lonely and hunted**.

**Big idea:** science without ethics can turn genius into a menace.
keyTerms: science fiction — stories based on imagined scientific discoveries
invisible — cannot be seen
lawless — not obeying laws

sections.h: Griffin's discovery — and the science behind invisibility
sections.md:
**Griffin** is a scientist who has discovered a way to make the human body **transparent**. He swallows certain rare drugs, and his body becomes as transparent as a sheet of glass, though it remains as solid as glass too — he can be touched but not seen.

**How would that work, really?** We see objects because they **absorb, reflect or refract light**. Glass is almost invisible in water because light passes through and bends very little. For a body to be invisible, every tissue would need to have the same **refractive index** as air and absorb no light. Wells hand-waves the chemistry — that is the 'fiction' part — but the idea is based on real optics. (A fun puzzle: a fully invisible person would also be **blind**, since the retina must absorb light to see! Wells doesn't deal with this.)

**Important limits in the story:**
- He is **invisible only when naked**. Clothes, food in his stomach, and mud on his feet are visible.
- So he must go about **without clothes**, even in the **cold of a London winter** — he catches a chill and sneezes.
- That's why the boys see the **muddy footprints**: his feet, freshly washed in a puddle? — no, they are footprints because he has just stepped in mud, and the mud stays visible.

check.q: Why could the boys see footprints though they couldn't see the man?
options: His feet had mud on them, and mud is visible
check.why: Griffin's body was invisible, but the mud he stepped in stayed visible and left prints on the steps.

sections.h: London: fire, a cold winter and a department store
sections.md:
Griffin, a **rather unscrupulous** man, had been living in London. He had quarrelled with his **landlord**, who wanted to turn him out of his room. In revenge, Griffin **set fire to the house**, and to escape, he took off his clothes and became invisible.

Now he was **homeless**, without clothes, without money, invisible but **freezing** in the London winter.

He slipped into a big **London store** for warmth. When the store closed, he broke open boxes and wrapped himself in warm clothes. He found food in the store's kitchens and slept on a pile of quilts. Next morning, the assistants came in and found him — or rather, a fully dressed figure. Griffin panicked, threw off the clothes, and escaped by becoming invisible again, **stark naked** in the cold once more.

Next he went to a **theatrical company's shop** in **Drury Lane** (London's theatre district). There he found a **false nose**, **dark glasses**, **bandages**, **whiskers** and a **wide-brimmed hat**, so that he could appear in public without revealing his invisibility. To escape, he **attacked the shopkeeper from behind** and robbed him of all the money he could find.

**Character note:** Griffin's actions are increasingly **criminal**: arson, theft, assault. His brilliance as a scientist is not matched by any sense of right and wrong.

check.q: Why did Griffin set fire to his landlord's house?
options: In revenge, because the landlord wanted to turn him out
check.why: Griffin was angry that the landlord wanted to evict him, so he set fire to the house and escaped invisible.

sections.h: Iping: the strange guest at the Coach and Horses
sections.md:
Wanting peace to work on a way to become **visible** again, Griffin travels to the village of **Iping** and takes two rooms at the local inn, the **Coach and Horses**. It is the off-season, and the landlady, **Mrs Hall**, is delighted to have a guest in winter — especially one who pays in advance.

But the guest is **very strange**:
- His head is entirely covered in **bandages**; he wears dark glasses and a false nose.
- He wears **gloves** even indoors.
- He has **whiskers** and a wide hat.
- He keeps to his rooms, works with bottles and chemicals, and is **rude and bad-tempered**.

Mrs Hall, being curious and friendly, tries to chat with him; he snaps at her. She tells the villagers she thinks he has had an accident that disfigured him. The villagers make guesses: a criminal hiding from police? A man with a terrible face? He is the talk of Iping.

**The comic tone:** Wells writes these village scenes with gentle humour — gossip, curiosity and misunderstanding.

check.q: Why did Mrs Hall welcome the stranger despite his odd appearance?
options: It was the off-season and he paid in advance
He promised to fix the inn
check.why: Guests were rare in winter, and the stranger paid in advance, so Mrs Hall was glad to have him.

sections.h: The clergyman's study and the burglary
sections.md:
Soon, **strange things** start happening in Iping. Early one morning, the **clergyman** and his wife are woken by noises in the study. They creep downstairs and hear the **chink of money** being taken from the clergyman's desk. They burst into the study, poker in hand — but there is **no one**. The desk drawer is open, the money is gone, but the room is empty. The clergyman's wife is certain she heard someone **sneeze** in the hallway.

At the same time, **Mr and Mrs Hall** find the stranger's door open and his room **empty** — but his clothes and bandages are lying about! How could he have gone out without clothes? As Mrs Hall stares, the **bed-clothes** gather themselves into a bundle and leap over the bed rail; the stranger's **hat** jumps off the bedpost and flies at her face; the **bedroom chair** springs into the air and charges at her, pushing the Halls out of the room, and the door slams and locks.

Mrs Hall is convinced the room is **haunted** — that the stranger has put **spirits** into her furniture. *My poor dear mother's chair!* she cries.

**Humour and horror mix** here: scary events described through a landlady's fussy concern for her furniture.

check.q: What did Mrs Hall believe after the furniture attacked her?
options: That the stranger was a magician
That the stranger had put spirits into her furniture
That her husband was playing a trick
check.why: Unable to explain the flying hat and charging chair, Mrs Hall believed the stranger had bewitched the furniture with spirits.

sections.h: Unmasked: the fight and the escape
sections.md:
When the stranger reappears, the villagers want an explanation. Mrs Hall confronts him, demanding to know why he went out and how he entered his room without passing through the door. He becomes furious and does something astonishing: he **removes his bandages, glasses and nose**, revealing — **nothing**. A **headless figure** in clothes stands before them!

The people in the bar **scream** and rush out into the street.

The village **constable**, **Jaffers**, arrives with a warrant to arrest the stranger for the clergyman's robbery. He tries to seize him — and finds he is grappling with a **headless man** who keeps on fighting. Jaffers holds on to the invisible wrist. Then the stranger starts taking off his clothes. A shirt flies off; the figure becomes **completely invisible**. People feel blows from an invisible fist; Jaffers is struck and knocked unconscious? — he is knocked down, and Griffin **escapes**, free and unseen.

**Ending meaning:** Griffin's invisibility gives him escape but not peace. He is a fugitive, hunted, hated and alone.

fig.caption: Griffin's journey in the chapter.

check.why: Jaffers, the village constable, came with a warrant and grappled with the invisible Griffin.

sections.md:
**Griffin — character sketch:**
- **Brilliant** scientist who achieved what no one had.
- **Unscrupulous** and **lawless** — arson, theft, assault.
- **Rude, ill-tempered**, secretive.
- **Lonely** — invisibility cuts him off from humanity.

**Themes:**
1. **Misuse of science.** Knowledge without moral responsibility leads to harm.
2. **Power corrupts.** Invisibility feels like power, but Griffin uses it for crime.
3. **Isolation.** Being unseen means being unknown and unloved.
4. **Curiosity and gossip** in village life (the comic side).

**Science-fiction features:** a scientific idea (invisibility) explored seriously; its realistic limitations (naked in winter, visible mud, visible food); consequences for society.

**Language corner:** words — *unscrupulous, eccentric, fugitive, warrant, constable, clergyman*. Notice the **passive voice** in reporting events (*The money was taken*), and **verbs of motion** for invisible actions (*the chair sprang, the hat leapt*) — a clever technique to show an invisible actor.

rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-footprints-wi.title: Footprints without Feet — Chapter Companion (part 2)
rd-school-c10-english-b.fp-footprints-wi.subtitle: Griffin's adventures scene by scene, the science of invisibility, character, themes and exam answers

sections.md:
The NCERT chapter is an adapted extract from H. G. Wells's novel *The Invisible Man* (1897). Here is every event, retold.

**1. Footprints in London.** Two boys in a London street notice fresh muddy footprints appearing on the steps of a house — but no one is making them. The prints are bare feet. The boys follow them until they fade. The 'walker' is **Griffin**, a brilliant scientist who has made himself invisible.

**2. How he became invisible.** Griffin had discovered a way to make the human body transparent, swallowed certain drugs, and become invisible. Clothes, however, remain visible, so he had to go about naked — in the cold of a London winter.

**3. The landlord's house.** Griffin had set fire to the house of his landlord, who had wanted to throw him out. Now homeless, he wanders the streets.

**4. The department store.** To stay warm he slips into a big London store at closing time. He spends the night there, wearing warm clothes, eating food and sleeping on a pile of quilts. In the morning the assistants find him, and he escapes only by tearing off the clothes and running away invisible again.

**5. The theatre shop.** In Drury Lane he enters a theatrical costume shop. He takes bandages to wrap his face, dark glasses, a false nose, big whiskers and a hat, so he can look like a person. When the shopkeeper hears noises, Griffin hits him from behind, ties him up and steals the money in the shop.

**6. Iping and the inn.** Disguised, he goes to the village of **Iping** and takes rooms at an inn run by **Mrs Hall**. He pays well, so she tolerates his rudeness and odd appearance; she thinks he has suffered an accident that disfigured his face. He spends his time in his room with bottles and chemicals.

**7. The clergyman's money.** Early one morning the clergyman and his wife hear someone in their study. They find the desk drawer opened and money taken, but no one in sight. They even hear a sneeze — but see nobody.

**8. The empty room.** The same morning Mr and Mrs Hall find Griffin's door open and his clothes and bandages lying about, with nobody inside. Furniture seems to move by itself; a hat flies at Mrs Hall's face, and a chair pushes them out of the room. She decides the lodger is a spirit or a witch.

**9. The fight.** When Mrs Hall and the villagers confront him, Griffin, in a rage, removes his bandages, false nose and whiskers, revealing a headless figure. The local constable, **Jaffers**, tries to arrest him. Griffin throws off his clothes and fights invisibly. He knocks Jaffers unconscious and escapes.

check.q: Why did Griffin go into the London department store?
options: To get warmth, clothes and food
check.why: Invisible and naked in winter, he needed shelter, warm clothing and food, so he hid in a big store overnight.

sections.md:
We see an object because light **reflects** off it, or is **absorbed** or **bent** (refracted) by it. Glass is nearly invisible in water because their refractive indices are similar: light passes from one into the other with hardly any bending. Wells's idea was that Griffin changed the refractive index of his body to match that of air, so light passed straight through him.

Modern physics shows why that is not really possible for a living person: the eye itself must absorb light to see, so a truly invisible man would be blind! Today scientists experiment with **metamaterials** and 'cloaking' that guides light around small objects, but this is far from a human invisibility cloak.

The story's footprints work as clever science fiction because mud and water still stick to invisible feet — a detail that makes the impossible feel real.

sections.md:
**Strengths:** brilliant, inventive, daring — he achieved what no other scientist had.

**Weaknesses:** arrogant, bad-tempered, selfish and lawless. He sets fire to his landlord's house, robs the theatre shop and the clergyman, assaults the shopkeeper and the constable, and frightens the Halls.

He shows how **power without morality** turns into danger. Invisibility could have been used for good, but Griffin used it only for himself. That is why he is often called a 'lawless person'.

**Other characters:** the curious boys (who notice the footprints), Mrs Hall (practical, greedy for his money, then frightened), Mr Hall, the clergyman and his wife, the shopkeeper, and constable Jaffers (brave but no match for an invisible man).

eccentric — strange in behaviour

sections.md:
**Themes**
- **Misuse of science** — knowledge must be guided by ethics.
- **Isolation** — invisibility makes Griffin lonely and miserable, not powerful.
- **Appearance and reality** — the bandaged 'accident victim' is really a criminal.

**Q. 'Griffin was a lawless person.' Give examples. (100–120 words)**
Griffin was a gifted scientist who discovered how to become invisible, but he used his discovery only for selfish and criminal ends. When his landlord tried to evict him, he set the house on fire. He sneaked into a London store and slept there. In a theatrical shop he struck the owner, tied him up and stole his money and clothes. In Iping he robbed the clergyman's desk and later, when cornered, attacked constable Jaffers. He had no respect for others' property or safety. So he was indeed lawless — a genius whose lack of morals made his invention a curse.

**Q. How did Griffin become invisible?** He swallowed rare drugs that made his body as transparent as a sheet of glass.

**Q. Why was Mrs Hall willing to tolerate him at first?** He paid in advance and generously, and she believed his strange looks came from an accident.

**Exercise topics:** how Griffin became invisible; the department-store and theatre-shop episodes; why the Iping villagers were curious; what would you do if you were invisible — a short creative piece.
